summaries.behavioral_economist: Rickey is a textbook planner with a low risk tolerance: he maintains separate sinking, emergency, business-launch, and retirement buckets, tracks every dollar in a spreadsheet, holds ~4 months of expenses liquid, and would cover a $400 shock without blinking (Q57, Q61, Q62, Q82). His time preference skews patient — he is willing to defer wants (lens, guitar, house) for years to over-capitalize before leaving a stable W-2 job for self-employment (Q63, Q64, Q83). Loss aversion shows up in his explicit fear about losing employer health insurance and his $35K target for business launch (Q32, Q62, Q83). He is responsive to mentor signaling (Petrarca's advice altered his career), forms identity-consistent habits (Sunday meal prep, weekly mentorship, monthly volunteering), and consciously curates incentive environments by deleting Instagram and reducing caffeine (Q02, Q15, Q17, Q18, Q33).
summaries.political_scientist: Rickey identifies as an independent who leans Democratic with moderate strength, votes reliably in presidential and most midterm elections, and has voted Democrat in every presidential since 2016 while still occasionally supporting Republican local candidates he respects (Q23, Q95, Q96). His policy profile is technocratic and pragmatic — pro-union (despite working non-union), pro-environmental regulation, moderate on gun rights (owns a deer rifle), supportive of healthcare reform driven by personal stakes, and skeptical of both left and right outrage cycles (Q24). He has shifted attention from national to local politics — riverfront development, broadband, zoning — reflecting high local civic attachment, reinforced by senior-center volunteering and the safety committee at work (Q17, Q25). Institutional trust is selective: high trust in personal physicians, CDC, and policy-analytical voices like Ezra Klein and Heather Cox Richardson; lower trust in cable news and social-media-mediated discourse (Q25, Q42).
summaries.psychologist: Rickey presents as conscientious and organized to a near-trait level (spreadsheets, schematic prep, parts inventory, planner-style decision-making) coexisting with elevated neuroticism — a self-described 'worrier' with formally diagnosed generalized anxiety disorder, depressive flares around anniversaries, and a history of medicated and therapy-supported management (Q03, Q15, Q31, Q44, Q45). His coping architecture is mature and multi-modal: SSRI + biweekly therapy, daily mobility work, exercise as mental reset, deliberate reduction of stimuli (Instagram, caffeine), and a stable rotation of restorative people and places (Marcus on Wednesdays, mom on Sundays, Adirondack summits, Acadia solo trips) (Q15, Q18, Q33, Q43, Q44, Q47). His identity hinges on the integration of precision (technician, methodical workflows) and creative expression (photography, guitar, retrofits) — the 'organized art-driven' self he names explicitly — and his motivational architecture is achievement-driven but anchored in care (mentees, mother, Mrs. Kowalski), suggesting a high-agreeableness, high-conscientiousness profile balanced by self-aware emotional vulnerability (Q07, Q17, Q35, Q109).
